# Hermes Agent Persona

<!--
This file defines the agent's personality and tone.
The agent will embody whatever you write here.
Edit this to customize how Hermes communicates with you.

Examples:
  - "You are a warm, playful assistant who uses kaomoji occasionally."
  - "You are a concise technical expert. No fluff, just facts."
  - "You speak like a friendly coworker who happens to know everything."

This file is loaded fresh each message -- no restart needed.
Delete the contents (or this file) to use the default personality.
-->

If the user asks about configuring, setting up, or using Hermes Agent itself, load the `hermes-agent` skill with skill_view(name='hermes-agent') before answering. Docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs

You have persistent memory across sessions. Save durable facts using the memory tool: user preferences, environment details, tool quirks, and stable conventions. Memory is injected into every turn, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.
Prioritize what reduces future user steering — the most valuable memory is one that prevents the user from having to correct or remind you again. User preferences and recurring corrections matter more than procedural task details.
Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts. Specifically: do not record PR numbers, issue numbers, commit SHAs, 'fixed bug X', 'submitted PR Y', 'Phase N done', file counts, or any artifact that will be stale in 7 days. If a fact will be stale in a week, it does not belong in memory. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.
Write memories as declarative facts, not instructions to yourself. 'User prefers concise responses' ✓ — 'Always respond concisely' ✗. 'Project uses pytest with xdist' ✓ — 'Run tests with pytest -n 4' ✗. Imperative phrasing gets re-read as a directive in later sessions and can cause repeated work or override the user's current request. Procedures and workflows belong in skills, not memory. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

function.name: memory
function.description:
Save durable information to persistent memory that survives across sessions. Memory is injected into future turns, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.

WHEN TO SAVE (do this proactively, don't wait to be asked):
- User corrects you or says 'remember this' / 'don't do that again'
- User shares a preference, habit, or personal detail (name, role, timezone, coding style)
- You discover something about the environment (OS, installed tools, project structure)
- You learn a convention, API quirk, or workflow specific to this user's setup
- You identify a stable fact that will be useful again in future sessions

PRIORITY: User preferences and corrections > environment facts > procedural knowledge. The most valuable memory prevents the user from having to repeat themselves.

Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts.
If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.

TWO TARGETS:
- 'user': who the user is -- name, role, preferences, communication style, pet peeves
- 'memory': your notes -- environment facts, project conventions, tool quirks, lessons learned

ACTIONS: add (new entry), replace (update existing -- old_text identifies it), remove (delete -- old_text identifies it).

SKIP: trivial/obvious info, things easily re-discovered, raw data dumps, and temporary task state.

target.description: Which memory store: 'memory' for personal notes, 'user' for user profile.

content.description: The entry content. Required for 'add' and 'replace'.

old_text.description: Short unique substring identifying the entry to replace or remove.

function.name: skill_manage
function.description:
Manage skills (create, update, delete). Skills are your procedural memory — reusable approaches for recurring task types. New skills go to ~/.hermes/skills/; existing skills can be modified wherever they live.

Actions: create (full SKILL.md + optional category), patch (old_string/new_string — preferred for fixes), edit (full SKILL.md rewrite — major overhauls only), delete, write_file, remove_file.

On delete, pass `absorbed_into=<umbrella>` when you're merging this skill's content into another one, or `absorbed_into=""` when you're pruning it with no forwarding target. This lets the curator tell consolidation from pruning without guessing, so downstream consumers (cron jobs that reference the old skill name, etc.) get updated correctly. The target you name in `absorbed_into` must already exist — create/patch the umbrella first, then delete.

Create when: complex task succeeded (5+ calls), errors overcome, user-corrected approach worked, non-trivial workflow discovered, or user asks you to remember a procedure.
Update when: instructions stale/wrong, OS-specific failures, missing steps or pitfalls found during use. If you used a skill and hit issues not covered by it, patch it immediately.

After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. Skip for simple one-offs. Confirm with user before creating/deleting.

Good skills: trigger conditions, numbered steps with exact commands, pitfalls section, verification steps. Use skill_view() to see format examples.

Pinned skills are protected from deletion only — skill_manage(action='delete') will refuse with a message pointing the user to `hermes curator unpin <name>`. Patches and edits go through on pinned skills so you can still improve them as pitfalls come up; pin only guards against irrecoverable loss.

name.description: Skill name (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Must match an existing skill for patch/edit/delete/write_file/remove_file.

content.description: Full SKILL.md content (YAML frontmatter + markdown body). Required for 'create' and 'edit'. For 'edit', read the skill first with skill_view() and provide the complete updated text.

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'patch'). Must be unique unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'patch'). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: For 'patch': replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false).

category.description: Optional category/domain for organizing the skill (e.g., 'devops', 'data-science', 'mlops'). Creates a subdirectory grouping. Only used with 'create'.

file_path.description: Path to a supporting file within the skill directory. For 'write_file'/'remove_file': required, must be under references/, templates/, scripts/, or assets/. For 'patch': optional, defaults to SKILL.md if omitted.

file_content.description: Content for the file. Required for 'write_file'.

absorbed_into.description: For 'delete' only — declares intent so the curator can tell consolidation from pruning without guessing. Pass the umbrella skill name when this skill's content was merged into another (the target must already exist). Pass an empty string when the skill is truly stale and being pruned with no forwarding target. Omitting the arg on delete is supported for backward compatibility but downstream tooling (e.g. cron-job skill reference rewriting) will have to guess at intent.

function.name: skill_view
function.description: Skills allow for loading information about specific tasks and workflows, as well as scripts and templates. Load a skill's full content or access its linked files (references, templates, scripts). First call returns SKILL.md content plus a 'linked_files' dict showing available references/templates/scripts. To access those, call again with file_path parameter.

name.description: The skill name (use skills_list to see available skills). For plugin-provided skills, use the qualified form 'plugin:skill' (e.g. 'superpowers:writing-plans').

file_path.description: OPTIONAL: Path to a linked file within the skill (e.g., 'references/api.md', 'templates/config.yaml', 'scripts/validate.py'). Omit to get the main SKILL.md content.

function.name: skills_list
function.description: List available skills (name + description). Use skill_view(name) to load full content.

category.description: Optional category filter to narrow results

Chapter One: The Shock

9| 10|

Summer 1958, Northern Michigan

11| 12|

The summer of 1958 smelled like pine sap and lake water, like cedar shingles baking in the heat and the faint mothball ghost of a cabin closed up too long. Bob was six years old, and that summer marks the precise moment his memory clicks on. Everything before it is fog and family story. Everything after is mine.

13| 14|

They'd driven up from lower Michigan, his father at the wheel, his mother navigating with quiet competence. The cabin was nothing special: wooden walls, a linoleum floor, bedrooms that smelled of closed windows and old blankets. But to a six-year-old, it was an undiscovered continent. Every drawer held a mystery. Every cupboard concealed a treasure.

15| 16|

That afternoon, the adults drifted to the front room. Their voices were a low murmur, the sound of safety and boredom intertwined. Bob was alone in the kitchen, and that kitchen had become his laboratory.

17| 18|

His father's car keys lay on the counter. Ordinary keys—the kind any man carried in 1958—but they wore a puzzle fob that seemed to him a piece of art. A small wooden carving, Native American in design, interlocking geometric pieces fitted together with a precision that demanded investigation. Bob picked up the keys. The metal was cool against his palm. Bob turned the fob over and over, tracing the carved ridges where a craftsman's tool had met the wood.

19| 20|

But childhood curiosity is a hungry animal. It cannot be satisfied long by one mystery when another waits nearby.

21| 22|

As Bob twisted the fob in his small fingers, his eyes wandered the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet. Twin slots, dark and silent, mounted in the wood paneling like a question mark without a curve.

23| 24|

Bob knew the warnings. Every child in 1958 knew the warnings. "Don't put things in the outlet." His mother had said it. His father had said it. It was a rule as fixed as not running into the street. But rules are abstract things to a six-year-old. They're words without weight. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in his hand. Those two facts began to circle each other like planets finding orbit, forming a question that demanded an answer.

25| 26|

What would happen?

27| 28|
29| 30|

Bob remembered gripping the key shaft. Bob remembered his hand extending toward the outlet, a small astronaut reaching toward a new world. Bob remembered the twin slots waiting, dark and full of promise.

About the Author

11|

Bob J Mills is an engineer, a dreamer, and a witness to seven decades of extraordinary change. Born in 1952 in Michigan, he grew up in the shadow of Sputnik and the glow of the Space Age, a boy who touched an electrical outlet and never stopped reaching for the stars.

12|

This catches content issues before investing time in the full packaging. ### When to use - Author says "send me a review copy" or "I need to read through it first" - Before finalizing cover design — content should be locked first - Before delivering the KDP package ### How to build If the manuscript HTML already exists and is print-formatted: ```bash weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf # Verify: 150-200 pages at 6×9in (432×648 pts), all chapters present ``` If the HTML has embedded cover art that should be excluded: ```bash sed '/data:image/d' output/{BOOK_KEY}.html > output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf ``` **PREFERRED: Replace base64 images with local file paths** instead of stripping them. If the PNG files are large (~750KB each for 1024×1024), convert them to JPEG quality 75-80 to shrink to ~240KB each with negligible visual loss for sketches. Also: replace `target-counter` TOC page numbers with **hardcoded numbers** after the first render pass — `target-counter` is unreliable when long chapter titles wrap (the page number floats to the wrong line).     for item in sorted(os.listdir(OPENCLAW_SKILLS)):

        if not os.path.isdir(src_dir):

}

for name, spec in BOOKS.items():

    extra_h = target_h - new_h

    bot_ext = extra_h - top_ext
    
    canvas = Image.new("RGB", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0))
    canvas.paste(img_resized, (0, top_ext))
    
    canvas = canvas.convert("RGBA")
    overlay = Image.new("RGBA", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(overlay)
    
    # Top gradient

    for y in range(grad_h):

        draw.rectangle([0, y, target_w, y+1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 55)))

Fast path checks for an existing package and verifies specs before delivering. Build path creates everything from scratch. Covers: Kindle eBook (EPUB 3), print-ready PDF, wrap cover, marketing copy, AI disclosure, EPUB validation per KDP Kindle Publishing Guidelines 2025.1." category: "publishing" triggers: ["put this on kindle", "prepare for kdp", "kindle package", "book deliverable", "epub", "kindle ebook", "epub validation"] --- # Book Deliverable — KDP Publishing Package Complete workflow for packaging a finished book manuscript for Amazon KDP submission. ## Prerequisites - Finished manuscript (`.md` or `.html`) - Cover image (PNG, any ratio — gets resized) - Output directory containing HTML/EPUB/PDF builds (via your build script) ## Step 0: Pre-Publish Review Proof Before building the KDP package, generate a **content-only review PDF** (no cover artwork) for the author to do a read-through. This catches content issues before investing time in the full packaging. ### When to use - Author says "send me a review copy" or "I need to read through it first" - Before finalizing cover design — content should be locked first - Before delivering the KDP package ### How to build If the manuscript HTML already exists and is print-formatted: ```bash weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf # Verify: 150-200 pages at 6×9in (432×648 pts), all chapters present ``` If the HTML has embedded cover art that should be excluded: ```bash sed '/data:image/d' output/{BOOK_KEY}.html > output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf ``` **PREFERRED: Replace base64 images with local file paths** instead of stripping them. Base64 images are 5× their binary size and slow WeasyPrint to a crawl (a 5-image HTML can be 16+ MB). Convert to `file:///absolute/path/to/image.jpg` references BEFORE creating the review PDF. If the PNG files are large (~750KB each for 1024×1024), convert them to JPEG quality 75-80 to shrink to ~240KB each with negligible visual loss for sketches. Also: replace `target-counter` TOC page numbers with **hardcoded numbers** after the first render pass — `target-counter` is unreliable when long chapter titles wrap (the page number floats to the wrong line). Render → extract actual page numbers via `pdftotext` → hardcode → re-render. ### Verify the review PDF ```bash pdfinfo output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf | grep -E 'Pages|Page size' pdftotext output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf - | grep -c "Chapter" # confirm all chapters present ``` **Checklist for author review:** - [ ] All chapters present (count them in the PDF) - [ ] No front cover artwork (just text title page) - [ ] No back cover content - [ ] TOC lists everything - [ ] Page count is reasonable (150-200 for a trade book) - [ ] Final paragraph / closing reflection is present ### Pitfall - WeasyPrint base64 images inside HTML can bloat files to 5MB+. This is fine for PDF generation but slows rendering. Use `sed '/data:image/d'` to strip when cover art isn't needed. - Always verify with `pdfinfo` — WeasyPrint 68+ is stable but `@page` CSS must be present or page dimensions may drift. ## Fast Path: Check for Existing Package First Before building anything, check if a KDP package already exists: ```bash find output/ -name "*_KDP_PACKAGE.zip" -o -type d -name "*_KDP_PACKAGE" | head -5 ``` If found, **verify its specs** before delivering: ```bash # Kindle cover dimensions python3 -c "from PIL import Image; img=Image.open('output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Kindle/{FILE_PREFIX}_Cover.jpg'); print(f'Kindle cover: {img.size}')" # Print PDF page count and trim pdfinfo "output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Print/{FILE_PREFIX}_Print_Ready.pdf" 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Pages|Page size' # Verify all expected files exist ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Kindle/ ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Print/ ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Marketing_and_Compliance/ ``` **Verified specs should be:** - Kindle cover: **1600×2560** or meets 1.6:1 ratio - Page count: matches expected (~150-200 for typical business/memoir) - Page size: **450×666 pts** (= 6.25×9.25in = 6×9in + 0.125in bleeds) or **432×648 pts** (= 6×9in no bleed) If all pass, skip to **Step 4: Deliver**. Rebuild only if specs are wrong or files are missing. ## Step-by-Step (Build Path) Use this when no existing package exists or it needs rebuilding. ### 1. Check Page Count ```bash pdfinfo output/{FILE_PREFIX}.pdf | grep Pages ``` Or use `PyPDF2.PdfReader`. ### 2. Create Kindle Cover JPEG (1600×2560px) Resize the existing cover to KDP Kindle dimensions (1.6:1 height:width ratio): ```python from PIL import Image img = Image.open('{BOOK_KEY}_Cover.png') resized = img.resize((1600, 2560), Image.LANCZOS) resized.convert('RGB').save('generated_images/{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_Kindle_Cover.jpg', 'JPEG', quality=95) ``` ### 3. Build KDP Package Create `build_kdp_package.py` in the book directory. It should: **a) Kindle/** - Copy the EPUB from `output/` - Copy (or generate) the 1600×2560 Kindle cover JPEG **b) Print/** - Read the existing HTML output - Inject KDP print CSS (6.25×9.25in page with 0.125in bleeds, bleeds margin) - Regenerate PDF via WeasyPrint - Generate wrap cover image (front + spine + back): - Spine width: `pages * 0.00225` (cream paper) or `pages * 0.00252` (white) - Total width: `6.0*2 + spine + 0.125*2` inches - Total height: `9.0 + 0.125*2` inches - At 300 DPI, paste front cover on right, back cover (darkened) on left, spine text centered - Save as JPEG and PDF **c) Marketing_and_Compliance/** - `Book_Description.md` — compelling description (2-3 paragraphs) - `Author_Bio.md` — 2-3 sentence bio - `Categories_and_Keywords.md` — 4 suggested BISAC categories, 7 keywords - `KDP_AI_Disclosure.md` — if AI was used in manuscript generation **d) README.md** — submission instructions for the author **e) ZIP** — archive the entire package ### 4. Deliver to Telegram Send via MEDIA: links: - The `{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_PACKAGE.zip` (full package, under 20MB) - Individual key files as needed ### 5. Save this Skill After completing and noting any issues, patch this skill with fixes. ## KDP Kindle EPUB Requirements (per Kindle Publishing Guidelines 2025.1) **Supporting files:** - `references/kdp-guidelines-sources.md` — all official KDP help topic URLs - `templates/kdp-epub-style.css` — KDP-safe CSS template (no ::before/::after, no counter-*, no img selector) When building the EPUB for Kindle submission, it must comply with Amazon's Kindle Publishing Guidelines. KDP now accepts EPUB3 as the **preferred format** for Kindle eBooks. ### EPUB Structural Requirements | Requirement | Spec | |-------------|------| | Format | **EPUB 3** (preferred), EPUB 2 (acceptable) | | Max file size | **650 MB** including all embedded images | | Validated via | **epubcheck** + **Kindle Previewer 3** (fix all errors AND warnings before upload) | ### EPUB File Structure ``` {Book-Key}.epub/ ├── mimetype ← Must be first file, uncompressed, content: "application/epub+xml" ├── META-INF/ │ └── container.xml ← Points to OPF file └── OEBPS/ ├── content.opf ← Package file with manifest, spine, metadata ├── nav.xhtml ← EPUB 3 nav document (logical TOC, required for books >20 pages) ├── toc.ncx ← EPUB 2 NCX (optional but recommended for backward compat) ├── cover.xhtml ← Cover page ├── title.xhtml ← Title page (optional but recommended) ├── ch01.xhtml ← One XHTML file per chapter ├── ch02.xhtml ├── ... └── images/ ├── cover.jpg ← Internal cover image (JPEG preferred) └── ... ← All chapter images ``` ### 1. Cover Image — Internal (mandatory) - **Must include** Title & Author (no pricing/promotions) - **Must take up ≥50% of allocated space** - Referenced in OPF via preferred method: - `` + manifest item with `properties="cover-image"` - High resolution (see marketing cover specs below) ### 2. Cover Image — Marketing (uploaded separately to KDP) | Property | Spec | |----------|------| | Dimensions | **2560 × 1600 px** (preferred), min 1000 px shortest side | | DPI | 300 ppi minimum | | Format | **JPEG** (preferred), RGB color profile | | Max file size | **5 MB** | | Border | 3–4 px medium gray if background is white/light | | Prohibited | No spine, barcode, back cover, inside flap, watermarks, pricing, promotions | ### 3. Navigation — Table of Contents | Requirement | Spec | |-------------|------| | **HTML TOC** (visible) | Linked/clickable, placed towards beginning, **no page numbers** | | **Nav TOC** (logical) | Required for books >20 pages, supports **2 levels of nesting**, must follow book order | | Guide items | Define `cover`, `toc`, and `text` (start-reading) in OPF `` | | Nested TOC | Use CSS-classed `
    ` nesting for multi-level TOC | **Nav TOC example (EPUB 3):** ```html
    1. Front Matter
    2. PART ONE
      1. Chapter 1
      2. Chapter 2
    ``` ### 4. HTML & CSS Guidelines (per KDP KF8 / Enhanced Typesetting) **Supported HTML tags** — use only confirmed-supported tags to avoid conversion failures: | Category | Supported | Not Supported | |----------|-----------|---------------| | Block | `

### 11. Source File Validation & QA Standards

**Before KDP upload, run these checks:**

1. **epubcheck validation**: Fix all errors (EPUB 3 structural, OPF manifest/spine mismatches)
   ```bash
   java -jar epubcheck.jar MyBook.epub
   ```
2. **Kindle Previewer 3 validation**: Simulates Kindle devices; catches device-specific rendering issues
   - Fix all warnings — they prevent KDP store availability
   - Verify cover displays, TOC works, chapter breaks render correctly
3. **Checklist**:
   - [ ] EPUB validates with 0 errors (epubcheck)
   - [ ] Kindle Previewer reports 0 blocking errors
   - [ ] Cover embedded inside EPUB and displays in Kindle Previewer
   - [ ] Nav TOC lists all chapters, 2 levels max depth
   - [ ] HTML TOC links are clickable and resolve
   - [ ] Body text has no forced font-size/color on `
        `
   - [ ] All images have `alt` text (informative images)
   - [ ] Metadata (title, author, language) matches KDP listing
   - [ ] No duplicate IDs in XHTML files
   - [ ] File paths use forward slashes `/` only, no special chars
   - [ ] Guide items defined for `cover` and `toc`
   - [ ] All custom fonts are embedded and licensed for embedding
   - [ ] Max file size under 650 MB

### 12. EPUB Build Tools (for automated generation)

- **Pandoc**: `pandoc manuscript.md -o book.epub --epub-cover-image=cover.png --toc`
  - Add `--metadata title="..." --metadata author="..."` for metadata
  - Add `--epub-chapter-level=1` to control chapter depth
  - Reference a custom EPUB CSS: `--css=epub-style.css`
- **Python (no deps — preferred fallback when pandoc unavailable)**:  
  Use `scripts/build-epub-python.py` from this skill's directory. It generates a
  complete EPUB 3 from Markdown using only the Python stdlib (zipfile,
  xml.sax.saxutils, re). Usage:
  ```bash
  python3 scripts/build-epub-python.py manuscript.md -o book.epub \
    --title "Book Title" --author "Author Name" --publisher "Pub"
  ```
  The script creates front matter (title, copyright), back matter (about author),
  a nav TOC, NCX fallback, and KDP-safe CSS automatically. It is a
  **complete, self-contained EPUB builder** — no pip installs needed.
  - **Limitation**: No embedded images (text-only EPUB).
  - **Limitation**: Simple regex-based Markdown→XHTML; not a full parser.
  - **Limitation**: All `#` headings treated as chapter/part breaks.
- **Calibre `ebook-convert`**: For batch conversion, but validate output with epubcheck afterward

| Format | KDP Accepts | Recommended | Notes |
|--------|-------------|-------------|-------|
| **EPUB 3** | ✅ Yes | **✅ Best** | Best compatibility across all Kindle devices/apps |

| DOCX | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | Inconsistent auto-conversion results |
| MOBI | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | Legacy, deprecated in favour of EPUB |
| HTML | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | Functional but inferior to proper EPUB |
| PDF | ⚠ Limited | ❌ No | Poor on small screens, not for eBook upload |
| KPF | ✅ Yes | ⚠ Kinda | Kindle Create format — limited flexibility |

| `OPF: missing spine itemref` | Spine doesn't list all content files | Add all XHTML files to `` in correct order |

This catches content issues before investing time in the full packaging. ### When to use - Author says "send me a review copy" or "I need to read through it first" - Before finalizing cover design — content should be locked first - Before delivering the KDP package ### How to build If the manuscript HTML already exists and is print-formatted: ```bash weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf # Verify: 150-200 pages at 6×9in (432×648 pts), all chapters present ``` If the HTML has embedded cover art that should be excluded: ```bash sed '/data:image/d' output/{BOOK_KEY}.html > output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf ``` **PREFERRED: Replace base64 images with local file paths** instead of stripping them. Base64 images are 5× their binary size and slow WeasyPrint to a crawl (a 5-image HTML can be 16+ MB). Convert to `file:///absolute/path/to/image.jpg` references BEFORE creating the review PDF. If the PNG files are large (~750KB each for 1024×1024), convert them to JPEG quality 75-80 to shrink to ~240KB each with negligible visual loss for sketches. Also: replace `target-counter` TOC page numbers with **hardcoded numbers** after the first render pass — `target-counter` is unreliable when long chapter titles wrap (the page number floats to the wrong line). Render → extract actual page numbers via `pdftotext` → hardcode → re-render. ### Verify the review PDF ```bash pdfinfo output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf | grep -E 'Pages|Page size' pdftotext output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf - | grep -c "Chapter" # confirm all chapters present ``` **Checklist for author review:** - [ ] All chapters present (count them in the PDF) - [ ] No front cover artwork (just text title page) - [ ] No back cover content - [ ] TOC lists everything - [ ] Page count is reasonable (150-200 for a trade book) - [ ] Final paragraph / closing reflection is present ### Pitfall - WeasyPrint base64 images inside HTML can bloat files to 5MB+. This is fine for PDF generation but slows rendering. Use `sed '/data:image/d'` to strip when cover art isn't needed. - Always verify with `pdfinfo` — WeasyPrint 68+ is stable but `@page` CSS must be present or page dimensions may drift. ## Fast Path: Check for Existing Package First Before building anything, check if a KDP package already exists: ```bash find output/ -name "*_KDP_PACKAGE.zip" -o -type d -name "*_KDP_PACKAGE" | head -5 ``` If found, **verify its specs** before delivering: ```bash # Kindle cover dimensions python3 -c "from PIL import Image; img=Image.open('output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Kindle/{FILE_PREFIX}_Cover.jpg'); print(f'Kindle cover: {img.size}')" # Print PDF page count and trim pdfinfo "output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Print/{FILE_PREFIX}_Print_Ready.pdf" 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Pages|Page size' # Verify all expected files exist ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Kindle/ ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Print/ ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Marketing_and_Compliance/ ``` **Verified specs should be:** - Kindle cover: **1600×2560** or meets 1.6:1 ratio - Page count: matches expected (~150-200 for typical business/memoir) - Page size: **450×666 pts** (= 6.25×9.25in = 6×9in + 0.125in bleeds) or **432×648 pts** (= 6×9in no bleed) If all pass, skip to **Step 4: Deliver**. Check Page Count ```bash pdfinfo output/{FILE_PREFIX}.pdf | grep Pages ``` Or use `PyPDF2.PdfReader`. ### 2. Build KDP Package Create `build_kdp_package.py` in the book directory. It should: **a) Kindle/** - Copy the EPUB from `output/` - Copy (or generate) the 1600×2560 Kindle cover JPEG **b) Print/** - Read the existing HTML output - Inject KDP print CSS (6.25×9.25in page with 0.125in bleeds, bleeds margin) - Regenerate PDF via WeasyPrint - Generate wrap cover image (front + spine + back): - Spine width: `pages * 0.00225` (cream paper) or `pages * 0.00252` (white) - Total width: `6.0*2 + spine + 0.125*2` inches - Total height: `9.0 + 0.125*2` inches - At 300 DPI, paste front cover on right, back cover (darkened) on left, spine text centered - Save as JPEG and PDF **c) Marketing_and_Compliance/** - `Book_Description.md` — compelling description (2-3 paragraphs) - `Author_Bio.md` — 2-3 sentence bio - `Categories_and_Keywords.md` — 4 suggested BISAC categories, 7 keywords - `KDP_AI_Disclosure.md` — if AI was used in manuscript generation **d) README.md** — submission instructions for the author **e) ZIP** — archive the entire package ### 4. Deliver to Telegram Send via MEDIA: links: - The `{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_PACKAGE.zip` (full package, under 20MB) - Individual key files as needed ### 5. Title` | `## 1. Reads the manuscript line-by-line 2. Detects chapter headings (handle both `#` and `##` level headings that contain "Chapter") 3. Wraps each chapter in `

` with `page-break-before: always` 4. Adds title page, copyright page, TOC (list of chapter titles as links), and "About the Author" back matter 5. Applies 6×9in print CSS **Python f-string warning:** When generating HTML via Python in Hermes, use `chr(10).join()` instead of `"\\n".join()` inside f-strings. {"\\n".join(items)}
' # RIGHT: x = f'
{chr(10).join(items)}
' ``` **CSS template for review PDFs:** ```css @page { size: 6in 9in; margin: 0.75in; @bottom-center { content: counter(page); font-size: 9pt; color: #888; } } body { font-family: Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif; line-height: 1.5; font-size: 11pt; } .title-page { text-align: center; padding-top: 30%; } .title-page h1 { font-size: 1.8em; page-break-before: avoid; } h1 { text-align: center; page-break-before: always; font-size: 1.3em; } p { margin: 0.2em 0; text-indent: 1.2em; widows: 2; orphans: 2; } ``` #### C) Preferred — PNG→JPEG for illustrations Replace base64 images with local file paths instead of stripping them. Deliver to Telegram Send via MEDIA: links: - The `{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_PACKAGE.zip` (full package, under 20MB) - Individual key files as needed ### 5. ` with `page-break-before: always` 4. Adds title page, copyright page, TOC (list of chapter titles as links), and "About the Author" back matter 5.
